papers.abstract_zh: 两项贡献研究了针对中枢神经系统 (CNS) 的病毒。对 69 名水痘带状疱疹病毒 (VZV) 中枢神经系统感染患者的脑脊液 (CSF) 进行的临床和蛋白质组学分析记录了头痛、发烧和运动/感觉障碍的主要表现。CSF 蛋白质组学显示,相对于对照,CSF 蛋白质丰度显着升高,上调的蛋白质富含 IFN-1 信号传导、细胞焦亡和血脑屏障 (BBB) 破坏途径。严重脑炎病例中的补体系统过度激活成为疾病严重程度的候选标志物和潜在的治疗靶点,强调了脑脊液蛋白质组学在识别可操作分子特征方面的价值。寨卡病毒 (ZIKV) 的多系统转录组学研究整合了来自受感染患者的人脑类器官、单核细胞衍生的树突状细胞和 PBMC 的数据,以绘制跨感染阶段的干扰素刺激基因 (ISG) 调控图谱。IFN-β 治疗有效激活了脑类器官中的 ISG,包括 IRF7 和 IFITM3,而单细胞转录组学揭示了 ISG 反应的细胞异质性。跨系统分析确定了 22 个共享 ISG,LASSO 回归提名了 11 个候选诊断生物标志物。功能性 siRNA 敲低证实 IFI35、IFI44 和 OAS3 限制 ZIKV 复制,将转录组学发现与经过验证的抗病毒机制联系起来。埃博拉病毒病 (EVD) 的机器学习和数学模型研究解决了关于 IFN-I 在疾病结果中的作用的长期争议。对 2014-2016 年西非流行病患者数据的分析表明,幸存者中的 IFN-I 反应先于症状出现,而非幸存者则在 3-4 天后出现相同的反应。这种延迟导致 IFN-I 和 IL-12 信号在非幸存者中重叠,从而破坏了有效 T 细胞激活所需的连续细胞因子线索。这些发现将时间免疫动态提升为宿主保护与病理的一个关键但未被充分认识的决定因素。登革热病毒 (DENV) 感染的综合代谢组学-转录组学研究使用 LC-MS 和 GC-MS 对 41 名患者和 23 名健康对照者的血浆进行了分析,鉴定出 197 种差异丰富的代谢物。通过 ROC 分析,建议将上调最多的物种(包括反式肉桂酸和左旋乙酰肉碱)作为诊断生物标志物。KEGG 和 GSEA 分析强调 ATP 结合盒 (ABC) 转运蛋白的破坏是一个关键的代谢扰动,GEO 数据集的转录组整合将 ABCC5、ABCB1 和 ABCG5 识别为中心目标,证实了这一点,为理解 DENV 诱导的细胞病理学开辟了新途径。一项针对 157 名 COVID-19 患者的纵向研究检查了不同疾病严重程度组中 TLR7、TYK2 和 OAS1 的表达。TLR7 低表达与严重程度和病毒血症密切相关,而 OAS1 在病毒载量较高的重症病例中持续存在,即使 TLR7 在恢复过程中下降。这些先天免疫基因的相互依赖性凸显了针对 SARS-CoV-2 的早期抗病毒反应的协调性和严重性分层性质,并对预后分层具有影响。一项研究探讨了转录因子 EB (TFEB) 和 E3 (TFE3)(溶酶体生物发生的主要调节因子)如何调节三种冠状病毒属的病毒复制、自噬和细胞凋亡:γ 冠状病毒 IBV、β 冠状病毒 HCoV-OC43 和 α 冠状病毒 PEDV。感染上调 TFEB/TFE3 并诱导溶酶体应激反应。TFE3 敲低揭示了其在控制复制和细胞死亡中的主要作用,在 IBV 和 HCoV-OC43 感染的细胞中具有协同 TFEB/TFE3 效应。Brefeldin A 实验进一步证实 HCoV-OC43 的流出是通过溶酶体途径发生的,从而将 TFEB/TFE3 控制的溶酶体生物学确定为跨冠状病毒属的保守宿主脆弱性。非洲猪瘟病毒 (ASFV) 的转录组学研究解决了其对原代猪肺泡巨噬细胞 (PAM) 的严格趋向性,而不是在永生化巨噬细胞系 (iPAM) 中的有限复制。SY-1 菌株的比较分析揭示了不同的宿主反应:iPAM 主要参与脂质代谢和氧化应激,而 PAM 则激活细胞因子信号传导和广泛的免疫效应程序。因此,iPAM 中复制的减少反映了根本不同的细胞环境,而不仅仅是受体的可用性。功能验证将 JPH4 和 CYP1A1 确定为候选宿主许可因子,为改进体外模型和抗病毒策略奠定了基础,鉴于缺乏获得许可的 ASF 疫苗,这一点至关重要。这七篇文章共同证明了集成多组学和系统方法解码宿主病毒相互作用的力量。交叉主题包括 IFN-I 信号传导的中心性和背景依赖性、时间免疫动力学的重要性、多组学整合在生物标志物发现中的实用性,以及适当的细胞和患者模型对机制研究的价值。我们感谢所有贡献的作者和审稿人,并希望该合集能够促进病毒传染病的新型诊断和宿主靶向治疗的发展。关键词:宿主-病毒相互作用、基因组学、转录组学、蛋白质组学、代谢组学、干扰素信号传导、先天免疫、病毒传染病、系统生物学、多组学

papers.title: Exploitation of host U2AF1 and U2AF2 splicing factors facilitates mosquito-borne orthoflavivirus infection across species.
papers.abstract: To identify novel host factors essential for orthoflavivirus replication, we performed proteomic profiling of endoplasmic reticulum fractions isolated from cells infected with Dengue virus or Zika virus (ZIKV). Among the enriched proteins, the splicing factor U2AF2 and its heterodimeric partner U2AF1 were found to be critical for efficient viral infection, functioning at the viral protein synthesis stage. The arginine/serine-rich (RS) domain and the first zinc knuckle (Zn1) of U2AF1, as well as nearly all domains except the RS domain of U2AF2, were essential for their proviral function. Disruption of the U2AF1-U2AF2 interaction potently suppressed ZIKV infection. U2AF1 and U2AF2 partially localize to the cytoplasm, and notably, the cytoplasmic U2AF2 was predominantly a truncated form that was sufficient to support viral replication. Both U2AF1 and U2AF2 bind to viral RNA, with U2AF1 binding being dependent on U2AF2. Interestingly, trans-complementation of the Aedes aegypti homolog u2af38 into U2AF1-knockout cells restored ZIKV replication, whereas expressing u2af50 in U2AF2-knockdown cells did not. However, knockdown of either u2af38 or u2af50 significantly inhibited the flavivirus replication in mosquitoes. Together, these findings reveal that flaviviruses co-opt host splicing factors in both human cells and mosquitoes, underscoring a conserved cross-species mechanism of viral exploitation.

papers.title_zh: 利用宿主 U2AF1 和 U2AF2 剪接因子可促进蚊媒正黄病毒跨物种感染。
papers.source_body_en: To identify novel host factors essential for orthoflavivirus replication, we performed proteomic profiling of endoplasmic reticulum fractions isolated from cells infected with Dengue virus or Zika virus (ZIKV). Among the enriched proteins, the splicing factor U2AF2 and its heterodimeric partner U2AF1 were found to be critical for efficient viral infection, functioning at the viral protein synthesis stage. The arginine/serine-rich (RS) domain and the first zinc knuckle (Zn1) of U2AF1, as well as nearly all domains except the RS domain of U2AF2, were essential for their proviral function. Disruption of the U2AF1-U2AF2 interaction potently suppressed ZIKV infection. U2AF1 and U2AF2 partially localize to the cytoplasm, and notably, the cytoplasmic U2AF2 was predominantly a truncated form that was sufficient to support viral replication. Both U2AF1 and U2AF2 bind to viral RNA, with U2AF1 binding being dependent on U2AF2. Interestingly, trans-complementation of the Aedes aegypti homolog u2af38 into U2AF1-knockout cells restored ZIKV replication, whereas expressing u2af50 in U2AF2-knockdown cells did not. However, knockdown of either u2af38 or u2af50 significantly inhibited the flavivirus replication in mosquitoes. Together, these findings reveal that flaviviruses co-opt host splicing factors in both human cells and mosquitoes, underscoring a conserved cross-species mechanism of viral exploitation.

papers.title: A Community-Based Infectious Disease Board Game to Enhance Intergenerational Learning in Gerontological Nursing Education.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop and evaluate a community-based infectious disease board game intervention aimed at enhancing intergenerational learning between nursing students and older adults, and improving competencies related to dengue fever, scabies, SARS, and HIV/AIDS. DESIGN: This quasi-experimental study used an independent, non-matched, two-group pretest - posttest design. METHODS: Third-year nursing students in southern Taiwan were recruited and assigned to either an intervention or a control group. The intervention group participated in a five-week program consisting of three weeks of classroom instruction followed by two weeks of board game - based learning sessions conducted with older adults. The control group received traditional lecture-based instruction. Outcomes measured included students' communication, teamwork, and social responsibility, as well as older adults' knowledge, attitudes, and preventive behaviors regarding infectious diseases. FINDINGS: Students in the intervention group demonstrated significantly greater improvements than the control group in health communication (t = 2.82, p = .006), team collaboration (t = 5.33, p < .001), and social responsibility (t = 4.07, p < .001). Older adults also showed significant improvements in infectious disease knowledge, attitudes, and preventive behaviors, all p < .001. CONCLUSIONS: The integration of educational board games into nursing curricula is an effective and scalable strategy for enhancing intergenerational learning, fostering key professional competencies among students, and improving health literacy among older adults. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This approach provides practical implications for gerontological nursing education by promoting intergenerational collaboration, strengthening community engagement, and supporting the development of preventive health behaviors among older populations.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 开发和评估基于社区的传染病棋盘游戏干预措施,旨在加强护生和老年人之间的代际学习,并提高与登革热、疥疮、SARS 和艾滋病毒/艾滋病相关的能力。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项准实验研究采用了独立、非匹配、两组前测-后测设计。

elements_zh.main_results: 干预组的学生在健康沟通(t = 2.82,p = .006)、团队协作(t = 5.33,p < .001)和社会责任(t = 4.07,p < .001)方面比对照组有显着改善。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 老年人在传染病知识、态度和预防行为方面也表现出显着改善,所有 p < .001。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 将教育棋盘游戏融入护理课程是一种有效且可扩展的策略,可增强代际学习、培养学生的关键专业能力以及提高老年人的健康素养。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 临床相关性:该方法通过促进代际合作、加强社区参与和支持老年人预防性健康行为的发展,为老年护理教育提供了实际意义。

papers.title: Evaluation of Escherichia coli-derived Silver Nanoparticles for Aedes Vector Control in Southern India
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus are the principal mosquito vectors in Tamil Nadu transmitting the major arboviral diseases such as Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika and Yellow Fever. Aedes aegypti serves as the primary vector, followed by Aedes albopictus. Due to the limitations and environmental concerns associated with predictable chemical larvicides, there is an emergency need for alternative and sustainable vector control strategies. METHODS: In this study, environmentally friendly silver nanoparticles were synthesized using Escherichia coli through a biogenic approach that develops the bacterium's naturally reducing and stabilizing properties. The synthesized silver nanoparticles were characterized for size, shape, and stability using UV-Visible spectroscopy and Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. The larvicidal efficacy of silver nanoparticles was evaluated against the larvae of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus from the Thiruvarur district of Tamil Nadu, India. LC50 and LC90 values were estimated using probit analysis according to Finney's method (Miller-Tainter approach) in SPSS. RESULTS: The biosynthesized silver nanoparticles showed strong larvicidal activity against both mosquito species, depending on the dose approach, the moderate larval mortality was observed in Aedes albopictus than in Aedes aegypti. The median lethal concentration (LC50) was estimated at 270 ± 16 mg/L for Aedes aegypti and 194 ± 13 mg/L for Aedes albopictus, and LC90 values were estimated at 3480 ± 490 mg/L for Aedes aegypti and 2510 ± 360 mg/L for Aedes albopictus. The findings indicate that the biogenically synthesized silver nanoparticles are an effective alternative to chemical larvicides, offering enhanced efficacy with reduced environment impact. CONCLUSION: The current study highlights the dual advantages of utilizing biological resources for nanoparticle synthesis and implementing sustainable approaches for the control of mosquito- borne diseases. Future research should focus on large-scale production, field-level efficacy assessments, and evaluation of potential effects on non-target organisms to support practical applications.

papers.title_zh: 大肠杆菌衍生的银纳米颗粒对印度南部伊蚊病媒控制的评价
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus are the principal mosquito vectors in Tamil Nadu transmitting the major arboviral diseases such as Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika and Yellow Fever. Aedes aegypti serves as the primary vector, followed by Aedes albopictus. Due to the limitations and environmental concerns associated with predictable chemical larvicides, there is an emergency need for alternative and sustainable vector control strategies. METHODS: In this study, environmentally friendly silver nanoparticles were synthesized using Escherichia coli through a biogenic approach that develops the bacterium's naturally reducing and stabilizing properties. The synthesized silver nanoparticles were characterized for size, shape, and stability using UV-Visible spectroscopy and Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. The larvicidal efficacy of silver nanoparticles was evaluated against the larvae of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus from the Thiruvarur district of Tamil Nadu, India. LC50 and LC90 values were estimated using probit analysis according to Finney's method (Miller-Tainter approach) in SPSS. RESULTS: The biosynthesized silver nanoparticles showed strong larvicidal activity against both mosquito species, depending on the dose approach, the moderate larval mortality was observed in Aedes albopictus than in Aedes aegypti. The median lethal concentration (LC50) was estimated at 270 ± 16 mg/L for Aedes aegypti and 194 ± 13 mg/L for Aedes albopictus, and LC90 values were estimated at 3480 ± 490 mg/L for Aedes aegypti and 2510 ± 360 mg/L for Aedes albopictus. The findings indicate that the biogenically synthesized silver nanoparticles are an effective alternative to chemical larvicides, offering enhanced efficacy with reduced environment impact. CONCLUSION: The current study highlights the dual advantages of utilizing biological resources for nanoparticle synthesis and implementing sustainable approaches for the control of mosquito- borne diseases. Future research should focus on large-scale production, field-level efficacy assessments, and evaluation of potential effects on non-target organisms to support practical applications.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:埃及伊蚊和白纹伊蚊是泰米尔纳德邦传播登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒和黄热病等主要虫媒病毒疾病的主要蚊媒。埃及伊蚊是主要媒介,其次是白纹伊蚊。由于可预测的化学杀幼虫剂的局限性和环境问题,迫切需要替代和可持续的病媒控制策略。方法:在这项研究中,利用大肠杆菌通过生物方法合成了环保型银纳米颗粒,该方法开发了细菌的自然还原和稳定特性。使用紫外-可见光谱和傅里叶变换红外(FTIR)光谱对合成的银纳米颗粒的尺寸、形状和稳定性进行了表征。针对印度泰米尔纳德邦蒂鲁瓦鲁尔地区的埃及伊蚊和白纹伊蚊幼虫,评估了银纳米粒子的杀幼虫功效。LC50和LC90值是根据SPSS中的芬尼法(Miller-Tainter法)使用概率分析来估计的。结果:生物合成的银纳米粒子对两种蚊子均表现出很强的杀幼虫活性,根据剂量方法,白纹伊蚊的幼虫死亡率低于埃及伊蚊。埃及伊蚊的半致死浓度 (LC50) 估计为 270 ± 16 mg/L,白纹伊蚊的半致死浓度 (LC50) 估计为 194 ± 13 mg/L,埃及伊蚊的半致死浓度 (LC90) 估计为 3480 ± 490 mg/L,白纹伊蚊的 LC90 值估计为 2510 ± 360 mg/L。研究结果表明,生物合成的银纳米颗粒是化学杀幼虫剂的有效替代品,可提高功效并减少对环境的影响。结论:当前的研究强调了利用生物资源合成纳米颗粒和实施可持续方法控制蚊媒疾病的双重优势。未来的研究应侧重于大规模生产、现场功效评估以及对非目标生物体的潜在影响的评估,以支持实际应用。

news.content: Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Search Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA Samoa Samoa Dengue Outbreak Response - DREF Final Report (MDRWS003) Format Situation Report Source IFRC Posted 16 Jul 2026 Originally published 15 Jul 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 4.39 MB) Description of the Event Date when the trigger was met 05-08-2025What happened, where and when? The Ministry of Health officially declared a dengue fever outbreak in Samoa on 17 April 2025, following a significant increase in suspected and confirmed cases, particularly on Upolu Island. As of the trigger date (5 August 2025), 7,970 clinically diagnosed cases had been reported, of which 2,743 were laboratory-confirmed. Between 4 and 10 August alone (epi-week 32), 1,974 new clinically diagnosed cases were recorded, including 116 laboratory-confirmed cases. The majority of cases (88 per cent) were from Upolu Island, with 55 per cent male and 45 per cent female. Cases were concentrated in the Apia Urban Area and Northwest Upolu regions, with the Faleata District accounting for 32 per cent of all cases. Individuals under 15 years old were disproportionately affected, comprising 72 per cent of all confirmed cases. Of the laboratory-confirmed serotypes, 91 per cent were DENV-1 and 9 per cent were DENV-2. The incidence rate was estimated at 620.7 per 100,000 population at the time of the trigger, with no signs of decline, indicating that the epidemiological peak was still ahead. Tragically, six dengue-related fatalities were confirmed during the outbreak, including children. Approximately 20 per cent of reported cases required hospitalization; of these, the majority were discharged following treatment, with no cases admitted to intensive care by the final weeks of the outbreak. The outbreak reached its epidemiological peak in mid-August 2025 (epi-week 32), when 2,090 new cases were recorded in a single week. The incidence rate reached 1,108 cases per 100,000 population by epi-week 30. By the end of the operation reporting period (epi-week 34), a cumulative total of 10,982 clinically diagnosed cases had been recorded, of which 3,379 were laboratory-confirmed (MOH Situation Report Issue No. 19). A sustained downward trend was observed toward the end of the reporting period, with epi-week 34 recording a 19 per cent decrease compared to the previous week; however, a Blue Alert remained in effect, indicating ongoing viral circulation. (Updated every 15 mins)BURSA:BMGREEN 1.990 ▲2.58% 14.09x |BURSA:DCHCARE 0.115 ▼4.17% 14.03x |BURSA:AIMAX 0.015 ▲50.00% 12.38x |BURSA:ESCERAM 0.170 ▲6.25% 11.98x |BURSA:NAIM 0.800 ▼1.23% 11.79x |BURSA:BMGREEN 1.990 ▲2.58% 14.09x |BURSA:DCHCARE 0.115 ▼4.17% 14.03x |BURSA:AIMAX 0.015 ▲50.00% 12.38x |BURSA:ESCERAM 0.170 ▲6.25% 11.98x |BURSA:NAIM 0.800 ▼1.23% 11.79x |HomeJapanese drugmaker Takeda's QDENGA becomes first dengue vaccine approved in IndiaCorporateWorldJapanese drugmaker Takeda's QDENGA becomes first dengue vaccine approved in IndiaBy Rishika Sadam / Reuters20 Jul 2026, 03:26 pmMake The Edge Malaysia your preferred source on Google (July 20): Japan's Takeda Pharmaceutical's dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India's drug regulator, making it the first dengue vaccine to be approved in the country, the company's unit said on Monday. The tetravalent live-attenuated vaccine, designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes, can be administered regardless of prior dengue exposure and does not require pre-vaccination testing, the company said. "The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades," the company said. Advertisement Takeda partnered with Indian vaccine maker Biological E in 2024 to expand manufacturing of QDENGA. Under the agreement, Biological E plans to build capacity to produce 50 million doses annually, supporting Takeda's goal of manufacturing 100 million doses a year globally by the end of the decade. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease that poses a significant global public health threat and India accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden, the company said. "Since its launch in 2022, QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed globally," said Mahender Nayak, head of Intercontinental markets. The vaccine's long-term data demonstrated sustained protection against dengue disease and dengue-related hospitalisation, Takeda said. news.content: Updated 20 July 2026 at 13:31 IST India Gets Its First Approved Dengue Vaccine: Takeda's QDENGA Gets Drug Regulator Nod As Cases Surge 11-Fold In Two Decades India has approved Takeda's QDENGA, the country's first dengue vaccine. The shot protects against all four dengue virus serotypes and comes as India accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden. Deepti Verma Health News 3 min read Follow : India Gets Its First Approved Dengue Vaccine: Takeda's QDENGA Gets Drug Regulator Nod As Cases Surge 11-Fold In Two Decades | Image: Reuters In a landmark breakthrough for public health, India has approved its first dengue vaccine, with the country's drug regulator clearing Japanese pharmaceutical giant Takeda's QDENGA for use. The approval marks a major milestone in India's battle against one of its fastest-growing mosquito-borne diseases. The vaccine, approved on Monday, is the first dengue vaccine to receive regulatory clearance in India and comes at a time when dengue cases in the country have increased 11-fold over the past two decades, underscoring the urgent need for preventive tools. Why This Matters For India The approval is particularly significant because India accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden, making it one of the countries most affected by the disease. Dengue outbreaks have become increasingly frequent, especially during and after the monsoon season, placing immense pressure on hospitals and public health systems across several states. Advertisement Health experts believe the availability of a vaccine could become an important addition to existing mosquito-control measures and public awareness campaigns. What Is QDENGA? QDENGA is a tetravalent live-attenuated dengue vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes, a key advantage since infection with different serotypes can increase the risk of severe disease. Advertisement According to Takeda, the vaccine: Protects against all four dengue virus strains. Can be administered regardless of whether a person has previously had dengue. Does not require pre-vaccination testing, simplifying its use compared with some earlier dengue vaccines. Has demonstrated long-term protection against dengue infection and dengue-related hospitalisation in clinical studies. Manufacturing In India Takeda is also strengthening its manufacturing footprint in India. In 2024, the company partnered with Biological E, one of India's leading vaccine manufacturers, to expand production of QDENGA. Under the agreement, Biological E plans to build capacity to manufacture 50 million doses annually, contributing to Takeda's global target of producing 100 million doses a year by the end of the decade. The partnership is expected to improve vaccine availability for both India and international markets. Already Used Across The World Since its global launch in 2022, QDENGA has received approval in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed worldwide, according to Takeda. The company says long-term follow-up data continue to demonstrate sustained protection against symptomatic dengue and dengue-related hospitalisation. What Happens Next? While the regulatory approval is a major milestone, experts say wider rollout will depend on pricing, supply, recommendations from India's immunisation and public health authorities, and integration into dengue prevention strategies. If deployed at scale, the vaccine could significantly strengthen India's fight against dengue, a disease that continues to affect lakhs of people every year and remains a major seasonal public health challenge. (With Reuters inputs) ALSO READ: Big Blow To TMC Ahead Of July 21 Rally: Calcutta HC Refuses To Lift ED Freeze On Rs 440 Crore Party Accounts Published By: Deepti Verma Published On: 20 July 2026 at 13:31 IST

India World Sport FIFA 2026 Data Health Opinion Science Entertainment Premium Videos Podcast Photos Visual Stories Specials TH Explains eBooks TH Games Newsletter Lit For Life The Huddle Home Sci-Tech Health India approves first dengue vaccine for individuals aged 4 to 60 years Takeda’s two-dose QDENGA vaccine, approved by the Drug Controller General of India, can be administered without prior dengue screening and is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypesUpdated - July 20, 2026 04:57 pm IST The Hindu BureauREAD LATER SEE ALL Remove The two-dose vaccine, approved for individuals aged 4 to 60 years, is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes and can be administered regardless of previous dengue infection |Image used representational purpose only | Photo Credit: File Photo The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) has granted market authorisation to Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India’s QDENGA (TAK-003), making it the first dengue vaccine to be approved in the country, according to a press release issued by the company. Vaccine for dengue may be available commercially by mid-2026 The vaccine has been approved for the prevention of dengue disease in individuals aged 4 to 60 years. QDENGA is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to provide protection against all four dengue virus serotypes and is administered as a two-dose regimen, with doses given three months apart.According to the company, the vaccine can be administered irrespective of whether an individual has had a previous dengue infection and does not require pre-vaccination screening. The approval comes as dengue continues to pose a significant public health challenge in India, where reported cases have increased nearly 11-fold over the past two decades. India accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden, although modelling studies suggest the actual number of infections is substantially higher than reported.The approval is based on Takeda’s global clinical development programme comprising 19 Phase I, II and III clinical trials involving more than 28,000 participants in dengue-endemic and non-endemic regions.The company’s pivotal Phase III TIDES (DEN-301) trial enrolled more than 20,000 participants across eight dengue-endemic countries. According to Takeda, the vaccine demonstrated an efficacy of 80.2% against virologically confirmed dengue 12 months after the second dose and 90.4% efficacy against dengue-related hospitalisation at 18 months. Follow-up data at 4.5 years showed 84.1% efficacy against dengue-related hospitalisation, while seven-year follow-up demonstrated sustained protection against dengue disease and dengue-related hospitalisation across all four serotypes. Landmark study offers new insights into what protects against dengueThe approval in India was also supported by a Phase III clinical trial conducted among participants aged 4 to 60 years. The company said the study found the vaccine to be safe, well tolerated and immunogenic in children, adolescents and adults.Takeda said QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries across Asia, Latin America and Europe, with more than 32 million doses distributed through public and private immunisation programmes. The vaccine is recommended by the World Health Organization for use in dengue-endemic settings with high transmission and has also received WHO prequalification. It is currently included in Brazil’s National Immunization Program and is available through public programmes in Argentina, Colombia and Indonesia. Explained | Why is a viable dengue vaccine not yet availableThe company said it would work with Indian regulatory authorities, public health stakeholders and healthcare providers to support the planning and availability of the vaccine in India. news.content: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages SearchSearch All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home Taiwan News Tue, Jul 21, 2026 page4 New antibody offers possible dengue fever relief By Lee I-chia / Staff reporter Add TT as Preferred Source A research team from the National Health Research Institutes (NHRI) and National Cheng Kung University (NCKU) has identified the mechanism behind the severe inflammatory response triggered by dengue virus infection and developed a bispecific antibody that blocks it, showing promise as a treatment for dengue fever. The research team was led by NCKU Department of Medical Laboratory Science and Biotechnology professor Wang Jen-ren (王貞仁) and NHRI Immunology Research Center Distinguished Investigator Hsieh Shie-liang (謝世良). The team said an estimated 390 million dengue virus infections occur worldwide each year, with about 96 million people developing symptoms and approximately 500,000 progressing to severe disease, resulting in about 22,000 deaths annually. National Health Research Institutes president Sytwu Huey-kang, second from right, poses for a photograph with other experts during a news conference in the Ministry of Health and Welfare in Taipei yesterday. Photo: CNA In 2015, a DENV-2 dengue fever outbreak in Taiwan resulted in 43,000 confirmed cases and 228 deaths, the country’s largest dengue outbreak in decades. NHRI President Sytwu Huey-kang (司徒惠康) said at a news conference yesterday at the Ministry of Health and Welfare that dengue fever remains a public health challenge that is difficult to control. Patients might initially experience only a mild fever, but it is often followed by symptoms such as pain behind the eyes and joint pain, he said. In some cases, the condition can lead to dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. There is no vaccine to effectively prevent dengue fever, and clinical treatment relies mainly on supportive care, Hsieh said. During dengue infection, activation of immune cells drives excessive production of pro-inflammatory factors, contributing to fever, he said. The pathogenesis of severe dengue is widely believed to involve dengue virus-induced overactivation of immune cells, which triggers a cytokine storm. The excessive release of cytokines increases vascular permeability, leading to plasma leakage, dengue shock syndrome and organ dysfunction, he added. Hsieh said their study confirmed that the severe inflammatory response triggered by dengue virus infection is not driven by a single immune receptor, but by the combined action of two immune receptors.The team demonstrated that simultaneously blocking CLEC5A and TLR2 can effectively suppress the excessive inflammatory response caused by dengue virus. They designed and developed a bispecific antibody capable of targeting both receptors at the same time, he said. Wang said experiments showed that the bispecific antibody reduced various inflammatory responses associated with severe dengue caused by all four major dengue virus serotypes, as well as some strains carrying mutations linked to severe disease. The team said the antibody could be a novel treatment for severe dengue fever and might have applications against Zika virus and Japanese encephalitis. The NHRI said the research findings were published this month in the Journal of Biomedical Science. Separately, the Chiayi City Government Health Bureau yesterday confirmed the city’s first imported dengue fever case, involving a student who had returned from Vietnam. The student traveled to Vietnam during summer vacation and developed fever, headache and pain behind the eyes last Wednesday before testing positive for dengue fever on Saturday, the bureau said. The bureau sprayed the area within a 100m of the victim’s home, increased mosquito density surveys and removed possible breeding sites. It advised residents to eliminate standing water and take precautions against mosquito bites, especially during dengue season. analysis.brief_en: A Taiwanese research team from the National Health Research Institutes and National Cheng Kung University has developed a bispecific antibody designed to block two immune receptors (CLEC5A and TLR2) implicated in severe dengue inflammation, offering a potential therapeutic approach for the disease. The antibody demonstrated efficacy in preclinical experiments against all four dengue virus serotypes and certain severe-disease-associated strains. Globally, dengue causes an estimated 390 million infections annually, with 500,000 progressing to severe forms and 22,000 deaths. In Taiwan, the largest recent outbreak in 2015 resulted in 43,000 cases and 228 deaths. Separately, Chiayi City confirmed its first imported dengue case of the year in a student returning from Vietnam, prompting local health authorities to conduct mosquito control measures and public health advisories. While the antibody represents a promising advance, further clinical validation is required before potential deployment.

The antibody demonstrated efficacy in preclinical experiments against all four dengue virus serotypes and certain severe-disease-associated strains. Globally, dengue causes an estimated 390 million infections annually, with 500,000 progressing to severe forms and 22,000 deaths. In Taiwan, the largest recent outbreak in 2015 resulted in 43,000 cases and 228 deaths. Separately, Chiayi City confirmed its first imported dengue case of the year in a student returning from Vietnam, prompting local health authorities to conduct mosquito control measures and public health advisories. While the antibody represents a promising advance, further clinical validation is required before potential deployment.

news.content_title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
news.content: India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia. Japan's Takeda Pharmaceutical's dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India's drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO). The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it. The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections. In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died. Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic . Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes. Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal. Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems. Takeda's QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections. "The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades," the company said in a statement. Takeda estimates that India accounts for almost one-third of the global dengue burden. The approval follows a review of global and Indian phase III trial data involving more than 20,000 participants across eight countries, including Sri Lanka, as well as 480 volunteers in India. Regulators concluded the vaccine was safe and immunogenic in adults and children aged between four and 60 years. However, the CDSCO directed the company to undertake post-marketing safety and effectiveness studies in India within six months of the vaccine's commercial launch. QDENGA has already been approved in more than 40 countries and is WHO pre-qualified. In 2024, Takeda partnered with Indian vaccine manufacturer Biological E to manufacture up to 50 million doses annually, supporting Takeda's target of producing 100 million doses globally each year by the end of the decade. Dr Eng Eong, a dengue expert and professor in Emerging Infectious Diseases at Duke-NUS in Singapore, told the Telegraph that it was critical for India and other dengue-affected countries to move beyond strategies reliant on vector-control. "A licenced dengue vaccine [in India] adds an important piece to the very limited public health arsenal to combat dengue," he said. Shikha Taneja Malik, Senior Scientific Affairs Manager, Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative, South Asia, said: "A locally manufactured, affordable vaccine could meaningfully reduce severe cases and hospital strain. But there are still specific populations such as pregnant women, newborns, and older adults who would not benefit from this vaccine." Ms Malik said the vaccination should complement surveillance, vector control and development of new treatments to help reduce the burden of the disease. news.title: India’s first dengue vaccine approved: DCGI clears Takeda’s Qdenga for those aged 4 to 60
news.excerpt: The two-dose vaccine protects against all four dengue virus strains without requiring pre-vaccination testing, as India battles a rising dengue burden.

news.content: News Health and Wellness India’s first dengue vaccine approved: DCGI clears Takeda’s Qdenga for those aged 4 to 60 India’s first dengue vaccine approved: DCGI clears Takeda’s Qdenga for those aged 4 to 60 The two-dose vaccine protects against all four dengue virus strains without requiring pre-vaccination testing, as India battles a rising dengue burden. Written by: Anuradha Mascarenhas 4 min read Pune Updated: Jul 21, 2026 04:51 AM IST The approval comes at a critical time for public health, with reported dengue cases in India increasing 11-fold over the past two decades. (Image generated using AI) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) has approved Japanese company Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India’s dengue vaccine, Qdenga, making it the first such vaccine to be greenlighted in India. It is designed to protect against all four dengue virus strains (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4) and can be administered regardless of prior dengue exposure. It does not require pre-vaccination testing, the company said. The vaccine is administered subcutaneously. It comes as a two-dose regimen of 0.5 mL each, with doses given three months apart. The price has not been announced yet but since Takeda has entered into a manufacturing partnership with Hyderabad -based Biological E to produce up to 50 million doses annually, costs are expected to be competitive for the Indian market. Pricing will also depend on whether this gets incorporated into government immunisation programmes later. Also Read | Dengue is spreading fast: Can cutting-edge science outsmart it at last? The approval comes at a critical time for public health, with reported dengue cases in India increasing 11-fold over the past two decades. India continues to account for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease that poses a significant global public health threat, with prevalence in over 125 countries. India accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden. In an official statement issued today, Dr Mahender Nayak, head of Intercontinental Markets, Takeda, said, “Dengue is a growing public health challenge and India needs sustained, evidence-based prevention.” The latest seven-year data for Qdenga show continued protection against dengue infection and hospitalisation across all four serotypes — an important milestone for communities and health systems.” Since its launch in 2022, Qdenga has been approved in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed globally. Dr Goh Choo Beng, Medical Affairs Head, Southeast Asia and India Cluster, said, “India carries a substantial dengue burden, and all four dengue virus serotypes have been documented as co-circulating in several regions. The approval represents an important step in strengthening India’s comprehensive approach to dengue prevention, alongside vector control, surveillance, community awareness and other public health measures.” Also Read | Serum Institute of India ties up with DNDi for Phase III trial of dengue therapy What is the vaccine about? It is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It is approved for use in the four to 60 year age group, regardless of previous dengue exposure, without the need for pre-vaccination testing.It is the most extensively studied dengue vaccine, with long-term clinical data demonstrating sustained protection against dengue disease and dengue-related hospitalisation. Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads. What did clinical trials show? The approval in India is based on results from Takeda’s global clinical development programme, involving 19 Phase 1, 2 and 3 clinical trials with over 28,000 participants in both endemic and non-endemic regions. This included the pivotal Phase III TIDES (DEN-301) trial, which evaluated the vaccine in over 20,000 participants across eight countries over an extended period to evaluate both the long-term safety and efficacy of QDENGA. At 12 months following the second dose, the study met its primary endpoint, demonstrating an overall vaccine efficacy of 80.2% against virologically confirmed dengue (VCD). At 18 months, the study also demonstrated 90.4% efficacy against dengue-related hospitalisation, meeting a key secondary endpoint of the study. After 4.5 years, two doses of QDENGA provided 84.1% vaccine efficacy in preventing dengue-related hospitalisations. Notably, the vaccine has also shown sustained safety and efficacy for up to seven years across all four dengue virus serotypes. This approval is also supported by data from a Phase III clinical trial (DEN-302) conducted in Indian participants, which evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of the vaccine in the 4–60 age group. The study demonstrated that QDENGA was found to be tolerated, safe and immunogenic in healthy adults, adolescents and children. These clinical outcomes are further supported by real-world evidence generation and ongoing pharmacovigilance to deepen understanding of the vaccine’s safety and impact. WHO nod The vaccine has also received WHO prequalification, confirming it meets global standards for quality, safety and efficacy, and enabling eligibility for procurement through international agencies such as UNICEF and PAHO to support wider access. Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads. In 2025, reported cases exceeded 113,000, but modelling analyses suggest the dengue burden in India appears to be higher than reported, likely representing tens of millions of infections each year. © The Indian Express Pvt Ltd Expand Anuradha Mascarenhas Anuradha Mascarenhas is a Senior Editor at The Indian Express, based in Pune. India Gets Its First Dengue Vaccine As Cases Continue To Rise; Know Availability, Benefits And Key Facts What Is QDENGA? India Gets Its First Dengue Vaccine As Cases Continue To Rise; Know Availability, Benefits And Key Facts QDENGA, also known as TAK-003, is a live, attenuated dengue vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4). It is administered as two doses, with the second dose given three months after the first. Sunanda SinghUpdated: Monday, July 20, 2026, 02:03 PM IST What Is QDENGA? | India has taken a major step in the fight against dengue after the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) approved Takeda's QDENGA (TAK-003). The country's first dengue vaccine offers a major step forward in the fight against one of the country's most widespread mosquito-borne diseases. Developed by Japanese pharmaceutical company Takeda, the vaccine has already been approved in several countries and is expected to help reduce the burden of severe dengue infections. But what exactly is QDENGA?QDENGA, also known as TAK-003, is a live, attenuated dengue vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4). It is administered as two doses, with the second dose given three months after the first. FPJ Shorts Shambhu Sealed! Benefits of the vaccineClinical studies have shown that QDENGA helps reduce the risk of hospitalisation and severe dengue, which can lead to complications such as dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. While no vaccine provides 100% protection, it is expected to significantly lower the severity of the disease and reduce pressure on healthcare systems during dengue outbreaks. Unlike the older dengue vaccines, QDENGA does not require people to undergo blood testing to determine whether they had previously dengue.Availability in IndiaThe vaccine has already been approved in more than 40 countries, including the European Union, the United Kingdom, Brazil, Indonesia and Argentina. India now joins that list at a time when dengue is emerging as one of the country's biggest seasonal public health threats.Although the vaccine has received regulatory approval in India, it may not be immediately available across hospitals and clinics. Its commercial launch will depend on manufacturing, supply, pricing and distribution plans. Health authorities are also expected to issue detailed recommendations regarding eligible age groups and vaccination guidelines. Opens in new tabWion/India/DCGI clears Takeda's QDENGA, India's first-ever dengue vaccine: Full details insideDCGI clears Takeda's QDENGA, India's first-ever dengue vaccine: Full details insideEdited By Vinay Prasad SharmaPublished: Jul 20, 2026, 22:03 IST | Updated: Jul 20, 2026, 22:03 ISTRepresentative image. Photograph: (Magnific)Story highlightsThe vaccine offers protection against all four strains of the dengue virus and is approved for people aged four to 60, irrespective of whether they've had dengue before, meaning no prior testing is required before vaccination.The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) has approved Japanese company Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India’s dengue vaccine, QDENGA. It is the first such vaccine that India has greenlighted. The approved vaccine is designed to protect against all four dengue virus strains (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4) and can be administered despite prior dengue exposure. The company confirmed that the vaccine does not require pre-vaccination testing.The vaccine is given as an under-the-skin (subcutaneous) injection, administered in a two-dose regimen of 0.5 mL each, which is spaced three months apart. While pricing has not been finalised yet, but are expected to be affordable for Indians, given that Takeda has partnered with Hyderabad-based Biological E to produce up to 50 million doses annually. The final price will also hinge on whether the vaccine is eventually included in government-run immunisation schemes.The vaccine offers protection against all four strains of the dengue virus and is approved for people aged four to 60, irrespective of whether they've had dengue before, meaning no prior testing is required before vaccination. analysis.time: Published: Jul 20, 2026, 22:03 IST | Updated: Jul 20, 2026, 22:03 IST.
analysis.location_and_population: India; population aged four to 60, irrespective of prior dengue exposure; potential inclusion in government immunisation schemes.
analysis.event: The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) has approved Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India’s dengue vaccine, QDENGA, marking India's first-ever dengue vaccine approval.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The vaccine offers protection against all four dengue virus strains (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4). At 12 months post-second dose, efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue is 80.2%; at 18 months, efficacy against dengue-related hospitalisation is 90.4%. Long-term data at 4.5 years shows 84.1% efficacy in preventing hospitalisations, with safety and efficacy sustained for up to seven years.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The approval is confirmed by DCGI. WHO has also given a nod for the vaccine, confirming it meets global standards for quality, safety, and efficacy. Pricing has not been finalised yet but is expected to be affordable for Indians, given Takeda's partnership with Hyderabad-based Biological E to produce up to 50 million doses annually. The final price will also hinge on whether the vaccine is eventually included in government-run immunisation schemes. Ongoing real-world evidence and pharmacovigilance continue to reinforce these findings.

analysis.brief_en: On July 20, 2026, India's Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) approved Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India's dengue vaccine, QDENGA, marking the country's first-ever dengue vaccine authorization. The vaccine protects against all four dengue virus strains and is approved for individuals aged four to 60, regardless of prior dengue exposure, eliminating the need for pre-vaccination testing. Clinical data from extensive global trials, including the pivotal Phase III TIDES and DEN-302 trials involving over 20,000 participants, demonstrate high efficacy, with 80.2% protection against confirmed dengue at 12 months and 90.4% against hospitalization at 18 months. Long-term data shows sustained efficacy up to seven years. The vaccine is administered as a two-dose subcutaneous injection spaced three months apart. While pricing remains undetermined, Takeda's partnership with Biological E aims to produce up to 50 million doses annually, with affordability and potential inclusion in government immunization schemes influencing final pricing. WHO has also endorsed the vaccine for global standards compliance.

Every year, thousands of people assume that once they have recovered from dengue, they have little to worry about in the future. It sounds logical, but unfortunately, that is not how dengue works.Unlike many viral infections that leave behind broad protection, dengue is far more complicated. The virus exists in four different forms, known as serotypes or strains. An infection caused by one strain usually protects a person only from that specific strain, leaving the door open for infection by the other three.2/8India's first dengue vaccine: What you should knowIndia has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA (TAK-003), developed by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India, for people aged 4 to 60 years. Given in two doses, three months apart, the vaccine is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and does not require pre-vaccination screening. While it offers broad protection and reduces the risk of severe dengue and hospitalisation, no vaccine provides 100% immunity against every infection or strain. Experts say vaccination should be taken according to national guidelines and should complement, not replace, measures to prevent mosquito bites.3/8Dengue is not one virus, it comes in four different serotypesThe dengue virus belongs to a family called flaviviruses and exists as four distinct serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Although they are closely related, they are different enough for the immune system to recognise them separately.Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital, explained, "Dengue continues to be one of the most prevalent mosquito-borne viral diseases, particularly in the monsoon months. What many are not aware of is that there are four virus strains (serotypes) of Dengue. Once infected with one strain, long-term immunity is typically only established against that one strain. They may still become infected with the remaining three strains in the future, though."This is why someone who had dengue five years ago is not automatically protected today. If another serotype is circulating in the community, a fresh infection remains possible.4/8Why a second dengue infection can sometimes be more dangerousOne of the reasons doctors take repeat dengue infections seriously is a process called antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). Scientists believe that antibodies formed during the first infection may not completely neutralise a different serotype during a later infection. Instead, they may unintentionally help the virus enter immune cells more efficiently, increasing the risk of severe disease in some people.Dr Kumar said, "As a matter of fact, dengue fever can be more serious upon a second infection with a different strain of the virus. That's why it's still the best way to avoid mosquito bites, even after experiencing dengue."This does not mean every second infection becomes severe. Many people recover completely. However, doctors recommend taking every episode of dengue seriously, regardless of whether someone has had the illness before.5/8If there are four strains, can one vaccine really protect against all of them?This is where dengue vaccination becomes more complex than vaccines for many other viral diseases.An ideal dengue vaccine needs to generate strong and balanced protection against all four serotypes. That is why dengue vaccines have undergone extensive evaluation, and different countries recommend different vaccines for different groups of people.Dr Kumar explained, "There is also a lot of debate as to whether one dengue vaccine will be sufficient to protect against all strains. The solution is not as simple as it sounds. Complete protection is required from all four strains of the dengue virus in an ideal vaccine, as incomplete protection may not be adequate."He further added, "Currently, guidelines for the use of dengue vaccines differ from country to country and are based on age, prior dengue infection, disease burden, and which vaccine is approved. Thus, vaccination should only be done after consulting a competent health expert and following the national health guidelines."6/8Even after vaccination, mosquito protection remains essentialDr Kumar said, "It is important to recognize that a vaccine is not 100% effective in eradicating the risk of dengue. Simple preventive measures are also as important."He advised, "Individuals should be protected from the bite of mosquitoes by using mosquito repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothes, using mosquito nets while sleeping, and ensuring that there is no stagnant water around the house where mosquitoes can breed."Sometimes, preventing dengue begins with something as simple as emptying a forgotten flower pot tray or covering a water storage container. These small habits can interrupt the breeding cycle of Aedes mosquitoes before they spread infection.7/8Know the warning signs, and don't wait for symptoms to worsenDengue often starts with symptoms that resemble many other viral illnesses. But timely diagnosis can make a significant difference, especially when hydration and medical monitoring are started early.Dr Kumar said, "If they start to become ill with a high fever, a very bad headache, a headache behind the eyes, joint pain, nausea, vomiting or rashes, they should go to the doctor immediately. The earlier the diagnosis, the better to prevent complications when it comes to hydration and timely medical care."He added, "Dengue can be treated successfully if recognised in time, but if not, it can worsen to a serious illness."8/8Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital.Inputs were used to explain why dengue infection does not provide protection against all virus strains, why repeat infections can still occur, and why vaccination should be taken only after consulting a qualified healthcare professional.Follow Us On Social MediaPhotostoriesFrom having no work for three years after quitting Sasural Simar Ka to wife Dipika Kakar supporting him financially; When Shoaib Ibrahim spoke about his struggles, career and lifeIndia approves dengue vaccine: Doctor explains the four virus strains and why immunity remains a major challengeLoved 'The Odyssey'? analysis.brief_en: India has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA (TAK-003), developed by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India, for use in individuals aged 4 to 60 years. The vaccine, administered in two doses three months apart, is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and aims to reduce severe dengue and hospitalization. Public health experts caution that while the vaccine offers broad protection, it does not confer 100% immunity and should be complemented by mosquito-bite prevention measures such as repellents, protective clothing, mosquito nets, and eliminating stagnant water. Vaccination is advised only after consulting a healthcare professional and following national guidelines, as effectiveness may vary by serotype and prior infection status. The announcement follows recognition of dengue's complexity, where infection with one serotype does not provide immunity against the other three, and repeat infections can pose higher risks of severe disease.

news.source_body_en: India has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA (TAK-003), developed by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India, for use in individuals aged 4 to 60 years. The vaccine, administered in two doses three months apart, is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and aims to reduce severe dengue and hospitalization. Public health experts caution that while the vaccine offers broad protection, it does not confer 100% immunity and should be complemented by mosquito-bite prevention measures such as repellents, protective clothing, mosquito nets, and eliminating stagnant water. Vaccination is advised only after consulting a healthcare professional and following national guidelines, as effectiveness may vary by serotype and prior infection status. The announcement follows recognition of dengue's complexity, where infection with one serotype does not provide immunity against the other three, and repeat infections can pose higher risks of severe disease.

news.content: Free Press Journal e-Paper Get App Home Mumbai NewsFPJ ShortsEntertainmentBollywoodHollywoodTelevisionRegional Film NewsMovie ReviewsBusinessTechnologyGamesFeaturesWeekendLifestyleIndiaSportsSportVotViralEducationStudy Abroad Tech HomeMumbaiMumbai Dengue Alert: BMC Urges Residents To Prevent Mosquito Breeding As Cases Rise 27.8%; Know Symptoms, Precautions And Treatment Mumbai Dengue Alert: BMC Urges Residents To Prevent Mosquito Breeding As Cases Rise 27.8%; Know Symptoms, Precautions And Treatment Mumbai has reported 938 dengue cases till mid-July, a 27.8% rise from last year. The BMC has urged residents to prevent mosquito breeding, identify warning symptoms early and seek prompt medical care to reduce the risk of severe dengue. Amit SrivastavaUpdated: Monday, July 20, 2026, 11:15 PM IST The BMC has urged Mumbai residents to prevent mosquito breeding and recognise early dengue symptoms as cases continue to rise | AI Generated Representational Image Mumbai, July 20, 2026: Mumbai has witnessed a significant rise in mosquito- and water-borne diseases during the first six-and-a-half months of 2026, with dengue cases increasing by 27.8%. The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) has advised residents to prevent water stagnation in and around their homes to curb mosquito breeding and reduce the risk of dengue and malaria. Till mid-July, 938 cases of dengue have already been reported in the city.Most common symptoms of dengueDengue symptoms usually appear 4–10 days after the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito. ● High fever (sudden onset) ● Severe headache● Pain behind the eyes● Muscle and joint pain● Nausea and vomiting● Skin rash● Extreme weakness and fatigueWarning signs: Seek immediate medical care● Severe abdominal pain● Persistent vomiting● Bleeding from the nose or gums● Blood in vomit or stool● Difficulty breathing● Excessive drowsiness or restlessnessMost important precautions● Prevent mosquito bites by using mosquito repellents, wearing full-sleeved clothes and using mosquito nets or window screens.● Do not allow water to stagnate in coolers, buckets, flower pots, tyres or other containers, as these are breeding sites for Aedes mosquitoes. Dengue mosquitoes breed in stagnant clean water.● Drink plenty of fluids and get adequate rest if you have a fever.Expert adviceDr Honey Savla, Consultant – Internal Medicine, Wockhardt Hospitals, Mumbai Central"Dengue can quickly become serious if warning signs are ignored. Avoid self-medicating with painkillers like ibuprofen or diclofenac, as they can increase the risk of bleeding."Also Watch: Read Also Mumbai Sees 28 Per Cent Surge In Dengue Cases, 18 Pc Rise In Malaria Until Mid-July; BMC Intensifies... Treatment"There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Management mainly involves adequate hydration, sufficient rest, regular monitoring, and taking paracetamol for fever as advised by a doctor. Most patients recover with supportive care, but those with warning signs may require hospitalisation, intravenous fluids, and close monitoring to prevent serious complications."To get details on exclusive and budget-friendly property deals in Mumbai & surrounding regions, do visit: https://budgetproperties.in/ Follow us on Add FPJ As a Trusted Source

news.content: Tuesday, Jul 21, 2026 Search HyderabadTelanganaAP NewsIndiaWorldEntertainmentSportScience and TechBusinessRewind ... NRIView PointcartoonMy SpaceEducation TodayReviewsPropertyLifestyle E-Paper NRIView PointcartoonMy SpaceReviewsEducation TodayPropertyLifestyle Home | News | Type 2 Diabetes Raises Risk Of Severe Dengue Complications Review Type 2 diabetes raises risk of severe dengue complications: Review A review paper by diabetes specialists found that people with Type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of severe dengue complications. The authors recommended integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes care to reduce hospitalisation and improve outcomes in endemic regions By PTI Published Date - 19 July 2026, 09:00 PM Thiruvananthapuram: People with Type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of severe, life-threatening dengue complications, according to a review paper by leading specialists. The paper, which is slated for publication in the International Journal of Diabetes & Technology, calls for integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes care to better protect vulnerable populations in dengue-endemic regions. The findings of the paper were shared with the media on Sunday. Led by diabetologist Dr Jothydev Kesavadev, the paper was co-authored by several leading diabetes experts from across the country, along with Dr Niti Pall, President-Elect of the International Diabetes Federation, Europe. The paper was recently presented at the 14th Jothydev’s Professional Education Forum Annual Global Diabetes Convention held in Kovalam, while the publication was released by Kerala Health Minister K Muraleedharan. According to the authors, persistently high blood sugar impairs immune function and damages blood vessels, making people with diabetes more susceptible to severe dengue infection. They said such patients are more likely to develop an exaggerated inflammatory response, or a “cytokine storm”, which can result in dengue haemorrhagic fever, internal bleeding and, in severe cases, dengue shock syndrome, a potentially fatal condition marked by a sharp fall in blood pressure. The review recommends incorporating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes management, saying it could help reduce severe illness and hospitalisation among high-risk individuals. “People with diabetes represent one of the most vulnerable groups during dengue outbreaks. Integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes care has the potential to reduce severe illness and hospitalisation in dengue-endemic regions,” Dr Kesavadev said. The authors said integrating infectious disease prevention with chronic disease management could strengthen healthcare delivery and improve health outcomes for millions of people living with diabetes in regions where dengue remains a major public health challenge, the statement added. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Around half of the world’s population is now at risk, with an estimated 100 million to 400 million infections reported annually, according to the World Health Organisation website. news.title_zh: 2 型糖尿病会增加严重登革热并发症的风险:综述
news.source_body_en: A review paper by diabetes specialists has revealed that people with Type 2 diabetes are at a significantly higher risk of severe, life-threatening complications from dengue fever. The paper, led by Dr Jothydev Kesavadev and co-authored by leading diabetes experts, including Dr Niti Pall, President-Elect of the International Diabetes Federation, Europe, was presented at the 14th Jothydev’s Professional Education Forum Annual Global Diabetes Convention in Kovalam. The findings, shared with the media on Sunday, highlight that persistently high blood sugar levels impair immune function and damage blood vessels, making individuals with diabetes more susceptible to severe dengue infections, including dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. The authors recommend integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes care to reduce severe illness and hospitalisation in dengue-endemic regions. This approach could strengthen healthcare delivery and improve health outcomes for millions of people living with diabetes in areas where dengue remains a major public health challenge.
news.content_zh: 糖尿病专家的一篇评论论文显示,2 型糖尿病患者因登革热而出现严重、危及生命的并发症的风险明显更高。这篇论文由 Jothydev Kesavadev 博士领导,由欧洲国际糖尿病联合会候任主席 Niti Pall 博士等顶尖糖尿病专家共同撰写,并在科瓦兰举行的第 14 届 Jothydev 专业教育论坛年度全球糖尿病大会上发表。周日与媒体分享的研究结果强调,持续高血糖水平会损害免疫功能并损害血管,使糖尿病患者更容易受到严重登革热感染,包括登革出血热和登革休克综合症。作者建议将登革热疫苗接种纳入常规糖尿病护理中,以减少登革热流行地区的严重疾病和住院治疗。在登革热仍然是主要公共卫生挑战的地区,这种方法可以加强医疗保健服务并改善数百万糖尿病患者的健康状况。

news.content: News Lifestyle Health People with type 2 diabetes face higher risk of dengue, warns review; experts weigh in People with type 2 diabetes face higher risk of dengue, warns review; experts weigh in A review paper highlights why high blood sugar may increase the risk of severe dengue and the warning signs people with diabetes should never ignore By: Lifestyle Desk 4 min read New Delhi Jul 21, 2026 06:00 AM IST Let's understand alla bout diabetes and dengue link (Photo: AI Generated) Make us preferred source on Google Whatsapp twitter Facebook Reddit PRINT People with Type 2 diabetes face a higher risk of severe, life-threatening dengue complications, according to a review paper slated for publication in the International Journal of Diabetes & Technology , which calls for integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes care to protect vulnerable populations in dengue-endemic regions better. The study authors note that persistently high blood sugar impairs immune function and damages blood vessels, which makes people with diabetes more susceptible to severe dengue infection. According to the authors, such patients are more likely to develop an exaggerated inflammatory response, or a “cytokine storm”, which can result in dengue haemorrhagic fever, internal bleeding and, in severe cases, dengue shock syndrome, a potentially fatal condition marked by a sharp fall in blood pressure. DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine. Diabetologist Dr Jothydev Kesavadev led the paper, which was co-authored by several leading diabetes experts from across the country, along with Dr Niti Pall, President-Elect of the International Diabetes Federation, Europe. “In India, there are more than 100 million people affected by diabetes. And among diabetics, there is a close to 2-4 times risk of developing heart attack, stroke, and multiple other infections and complications. Despite treatment, in 80-90 per cent of people, glucose remains high in our country. In our recommendation, we have mentioned that the dengue vaccine should be a part of routine care in diabetes,” Dr Jothydev told indianexpress.com . Here’s what you should note. Dr Rajiv Kovil, diabetes and obesity specialist at Zandra Healthcare, said that this is not a randomised trial but a review of existing evidence. “International observational studies and meta-analyses consistently suggest that people with diabetes who contract dengue have a higher likelihood of severe disease and possibly death. However, association does not prove causation, and the risk may also reflect age, obesity, kidney disease , hypertension or poor glycaemic control,” said Dr Kovil. Story continues below this ad Symptoms to watch out for. The initial symptoms are similar for anyone with dengue and include high fever, severe body aches, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, and skin rash. “However, people with diabetes should be particularly aware if they experience persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, unusual drowsiness, bleeding from the gums or nose, reduced urine output, dizziness, or sudden weakness. They should also check their blood glucose more often because infections can cause unpredictable spikes or, in some cases, low sugar episodes due to poor food intake,” said Dr Vijay Negalur, HoD diabetology, KIMS Hospitals, Thane. Hydration is crucial (Photo: Getty Images/Thinkstock) Prevention Prevention starts with avoiding mosquito bites by using repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and getting rid of stagnant water around the home. Dr Negalur said that it is equally important to keep diabetes well-managed since stable blood sugar supports a stronger immune response . “Stay well-hydrated, eat balanced meals, and don’t ignore a fever that lasts more than a day or two. Anyone with diabetes who shows symptoms of dengue should seek medical advice early rather than wait for the illness to worsen,” said Dr Negalur. “Vaccination recommendations must follow approved indications and national policy,” added Dr Kovil. If someone with diabetes is diagnosed with dengue, are there any special treatment or monitoring considerations? Story continues below this ad Dr Negalur noted that some diabetes medications might need “temporary adjustments” based on the patient’s condition, appetite, and hydration status. “Timely medical supervision and regular monitoring of platelet counts, blood glucose, and overall health can greatly lower the risk of serious complications and support a smoother recovery,” said Dr Negalur. DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. news.content_title: India’s First Approved Dengue Vaccine: Takeda’s QDENGA Protects Against All Four Virus Serotypes
news.content: Credit: iStock SummaryThe Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) has granted market authorization for QDENGA to prevent dengue in individuals aged 4-60 years. According to Takeda, the vaccine can be administered regardless of previous dengue infection, without requiring pre-vaccination testing. Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India today announced that QDENGA (TAK-003) has become the first dengue vaccine to receive approval in India, marking a major milestone in the country's fight against the mosquito-borne disease. The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) has granted market authorization for QDENGA to prevent dengue in individuals aged 4-60 years. According to Takeda, it is India's first approved dengue vaccine and can be administered regardless of previous dengue infection, without requiring pre-vaccination testing. "Since its launch in 2022, QDENGA has been approved in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed globally. This approval marks an important step forward in strengthening dengue prevention in India," said Dr. Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets. The approval comes at a critical time as dengue cases in India have risen sharply over the past two decades. India accounts for nearly one-third of the global dengue burden. In 2025, more than 113,000 dengue cases were officially reported, although modelling studies suggest the true number of infections may run into tens of millions annually due to underreporting. Rapid urbanization, climate change and widespread mosquito breeding have made dengue a year-round public health concern. Since there is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue, prevention remains the most effective strategy. "India carries a substantial dengue burden, and all four dengue virus serotypes co-circulate in several regions. QDENGA is designed to protect against all four serotypes regardless of prior exposure," said Dr. Goh Choo Beng, Medical Affairs Head, Southeast Asia & India Cluster. The DCGI approval is supported by Takeda's global clinical development programme comprising 19 Phase 1, 2 and 3 clinical trials involving more than 28,000 participants in dengue-endemic and non-endemic regions. The pivotal Phase III TIDES (DEN-301) study enrolled more than 20,000 participants across eight countries and evaluated the vaccine's long-term safety and effectiveness. Key findings include: - 80.2% vaccine efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue one year after the second dose. - 90.4% efficacy against dengue-related hospitalization at 18 months. - 84.1% protection against dengue-related hospitalization after 4.5 years. - Safety and efficacy data demonstrating protection for up to seven years across all four dengue virus serotypes. The approval is also supported by an Indian Phase III (DEN-302) trial involving participants aged 4-60 years, which found QDENGA to be safe, well-tolerated and immunogenic in children, adolescents and adults. Read More: Dengue Is Spreading Beyond Monsoons And Into New Regions Across India, Says Expert QDENGA (TAK-003) is a live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It is administered as two 0.5 mL subcutaneous doses, given three months apart. The vaccine is built on a DENV-2 backbone, incorporating structural proteins from DENV-1, DENV-3 and DENV-4 to provide broad immune protection. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends QDENGA for use in dengue-endemic settings without the need for pre-vaccination screening. The vaccine is also included in the WHO List of Prequalified Vaccines, allowing procurement through agencies such as UNICEF and PAHO. The vaccine has been approved in 43 countries across Asia, Latin America and Europe. It is already part of Brazil's National Immunization Program and is available through public immunization programmes in Argentina, Colombia and Indonesia. The vaccine is approved in India for people aged 4-60 years to help prevent dengue disease. Takeda had partnered with Indian vaccine manufacturer Biological E in 2024 to expand production of QDENGA. Under the agreement, Biological E plans to manufacture 50 million doses annually, supporting Takeda's goal of producing 100 million doses globally each year by the end of the decade. End of Article

news.content_title: High blood sugar could make Dengue more dangerous for Type 2 diabetes patients, warn new study
news.content: Health News High blood sugar could make Dengue more dangerous for Type 2 diabetes patients, warn new study People with Type 2 diabetes are at a significantly higher risk of developing severe dengue, according to a new study. Researchers say persistently high blood sugar weakens the immune system and damages blood vessels, increasing the chances of life-threatening dengue complications. Ananya Sarma Updated On: 20 Jul 2026 01:20 PM Diabetes patients at greater risk of severe dengue, scientists warn in new study (Photo: Pinterest) New Delhi: As dengue cases continue to surge across tropical regions, scientists are drawing attention to a hidden risk factor that could determine how severely the disease affects a patient: Type 2 diabetes. New research suggests that people living with diabetes, particularly those with poorly controlled blood sugar, are significantly more vulnerable to developing severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening form of the mosquito-borne viral infection. The findings reinforce growing evidence that managing blood glucose levels may not only prevent long-term diabetes complications but could also improve outcomes during infectious diseases like dengue. People with Type 2 Diabetes at higher risk of severe dengue, study warns The latest research adds to a growing body of scientific evidence linking Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) with a higher risk of severe dengue. Researchers found that chronic hyperglycaemia, or persistently elevated blood sugar levels, weakens the body’s immune response while damaging blood vessels – two key factors that can make dengue infections more dangerous. Sponsored Links Sponsored Links Also Read ‘Nearly 100 US troops injured in last 2 weeks of Iran war’: Pentagon Bigg Boss 2026: Six editions, six hosts and one mega launch – Here’s everything you need to know Spain reclaim No. 1 spot in FIFA World Rankings after World Cup glory over Argentina According to the authors, high blood sugar impairs the function of immune cells that are responsible for fighting infections. At the same time, diabetes causes inflammation and injury to blood vessel linings, making patients more susceptible to plasma leakage, bleeding and organ complications that characterise severe dengue. Why diabetes makes dengue more dangerous Dengue infection itself can trigger inflammation throughout the body. In people with diabetes, this inflammatory response may become even more intense because the disease has already compromised immune and vascular health. Researchers explain that diabetes can: Reduce the effectiveness of white blood cells that destroy viruses. Increase chronic inflammation and oxidative stress. Damage blood vessels, making them more prone to leakage – a hallmark of severe dengue. Delay recovery by impairing the body’s ability to regulate infection and heal tissues. These biological changes may increase the likelihood of complications such as dengue haemorrhagic fever, dengue shock syndrome and multi-organ involvement. Good blood sugar control may lower risk Importantly, researchers emphasised that diabetes itself is not necessarily a guarantee of severe dengue. Evidence suggests that people with well-controlled blood glucose levels are less likely to experience serious complications than those with poorly managed diabetes. A 2024 review highlighted that patients with Type 2 diabetes who maintained recommended HbA1c levels did not consistently show a higher probability of developing severe dengue, underscoring the importance of good glycaemic control. However, scientists also caution that studies have produced varying results, with some hospital-based research finding a weaker association after patients received early medical care. Overall, recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses continue to identify diabetes as an important risk factor that warrants closer monitoring during dengue infection. What this means for people with diabetes With dengue outbreaks becoming more frequent in several countries, experts say people with diabetes should be particularly vigilant during mosquito season. Doctors recommend: Keeping blood sugar levels under control. Seeking medical attention early if dengue symptoms develop. Staying well hydrated and monitoring for warning signs. Avoiding self-medication with painkillers such as ibuprofen unless advised by a doctor, as they may increase bleeding risk in dengue. Healthcare providers may also monitor diabetic patients more closely during dengue infection because of their increased likelihood of complications. Dengue remains one of the world’s fastest-growing mosquito-borne diseases, affecting millions of people every year. As diabetes prevalence continues to rise globally, researchers believe understanding how chronic metabolic conditions influence infectious diseases will become increasingly important. news.source_body_en: A new study warns that people with Type 2 diabetes are at a significantly higher risk of developing severe dengue due to persistently high blood sugar levels. The research indicates that high blood sugar weakens the immune system and damages blood vessels, increasing the likelihood of life-threatening complications from dengue. news.content_zh: 一项新的研究警告说,由于持续的高血糖水平,2 型糖尿病患者患严重登革热的风险明显更高。研究表明,高血糖会削弱免疫系统并损害血管,增加登革热危及生命的并发症的可能性。News9live 报道的这项研究强调了控制血糖水平以改善登革热感染期间预后的重要性。这表明血糖控制良好的人出现严重并发症的可能性较小。这些发现强化了越来越多的证据表明 2 型糖尿病与严重登革热的风险较高有关,强调在蚊子季节需要保持警惕并尽早就医。
